concept: WiredTiger checkpoints and dirty-page write cost
summary: Source-anchored research for WiredTiger checkpoints and dirty-page write cost. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: Dirty pages contain modified cached data that requires reconciliation. Both checkpointing and dirty-page eviction can cause writes; checkpoint cadence alone therefore does not describe all background data-file write activity. (medium confidence) Sources: https://source.wiredtiger.com/develop/arch-eviction.html ; https://source.wiredtiger.com/develop/arch-checkpoint.html ; https://groups.google.com/g/wiredtiger-users/c/zNVzB6ZrYt4/m/YHjzWb2ECQAJ

WT-18765 reports that update-heavy test workloads accumulated dirty history-store content during the history-store checkpoint pass, when eviction skipped dirty pages in the syncing tree. The issue reports dirty-cache overshoot above its configured trigger. This is evidence for a specific mechanism, not a universal overshoot rate or an established fix. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-26)

Inference for shard-key evaluation (not stated by WiredTiger documentation): a checkpoint walks each btree and reconciles all dirty pages while skipping clean ones, so per-shard dirty-cache pressure, physical write activity, checkpoint duration and latency are reasonable measures to compare at the same logical workload. The WiredTiger documentation does not discuss shard keys or show that a better-balanced shard key reduces aggregate checkpoint bytes or infrastructure cost by a fixed amount. Sources: https://source.wiredtiger.com/develop/arch-checkpoint.html

Keep each eviction target below its corresponding trigger. The WiredTiger architecture guide states that for all eviction target and trigger sizes, the target must be lower than its trigger counterpart. Sources: https://source.wiredtiger.com/develop/arch-eviction.html

The dirty target and dirty trigger serve different roles: the target activates background eviction, whereas reaching the dirty trigger can throttle application threads and require them to perform eviction work. Treating both thresholds as checkpoint triggers confuses separate mechanisms. (medium confidence)

Cost-analysis inference (not stated by WiredTiger documentation): dirty pages must be reconciled when evicted, and application threads are throttled when dirty data reaches eviction_dirty_trigger, so per-node dirty-page pressure, physical writes and latency are reasonable measures for comparing candidate shard layouts. The WiredTiger documentation does not discuss shard keys, update locality or buffering effectiveness, and does not quantify savings from any particular shard key. Sources: https://source.wiredtiger.com/develop/arch-eviction.html

In the TurtleKV paper dated 2025-12-08, the WiredTiger random-insert experiment found little write-amplification improvement across approximately 16–500 MB of dirty-buffer allocation, with stronger reductions above that range. These are workload-specific experimental results, not production MongoDB sizing thresholds. (low confidence)

If background eviction cannot keep up, application threads can perform eviction before continuing reads or writes. Dirty-cache pressure can therefore increase request latency through foreground work as well as through checkpoint activity. (medium confidence)

In Percona's June 2020 benchmark, identified by the author as MongoDB 4.2.7, throughput fell from approximately 7,500 to 40 operations/second around checkpoints. After changing eviction settings it fell from approximately 6,700 to 1,250 instead. This is a historical workload-specific tradeoff: tuning reduced stalls but also lowered peak throughput, and does not establish a modern-version default recommendation. (low confidence)

Use time series rather than overall averages to assess checkpoint impact. The UBC researchers' WiredTiger performance-diagnosis study says aggregate metrics such as average throughput or latency conceal outlier events, and Percona shows this with 1-second throughput traces in which averaging had hidden checkpoint stalls. Percona's PMM guide also advises watching dirty pages in cache alongside checkpointing and checking WiredTiger block activity when investigating storage. Sources: https://people.ece.ubc.ca/sasha/papers/fse-2018.pdf ; https://www.percona.com/blog/2020/06/25/mongodb-checkpointing-woes/ ; https://www.percona.com/blog/2017/02/27/percona-monitoring-and-management-pmm-graphs-explained-wiredtiger-and-percona-memory-engine/

WiredTiger can trade dirty-buffer memory for write efficiency by retaining updates before flushing. Lower dirty occupancy is therefore not by itself proof of lower total write cost; the trade-off must include write amplification and application latency. (medium confidence)

The WiredTiger develop Page Deltas documentation retrieved on 2026-10-30 describes writing changed entries instead of full page images only for disaggregated layered row-store trees. It does not justify assuming that all MongoDB deployments support delta-only checkpoint writes; the architecture guide explicitly disclaims release-specific completeness. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

Checkpoints provide a consistent recovery point in the data files; the journal preserves intervening modifications for recovery. The previous checkpoint remains usable until the new checkpoint is published through metadata. (medium confidence)

The MongoDB manual describes writing snapshot data to disk as checkpoints at intervals of 60 seconds. This is a configured cadence, not a guarantee that a checkpoint completes within 60 seconds: Percona reported checkpoint times growing from a few seconds to a few minutes during a bulk load, and noted that a full checkpoint uses all available disk write capacity for as long as it takes. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/wiredtiger/ ; https://www.percona.com/blog/tuning-mongodb-for-bulk-loads/

Checkpoint reconciliation processes dirty pages and skips clean pages, including pages cleaned earlier by eviction. Dirty eviction itself reconciles modified pages, whereas clean eviction can discard the cached page without rewriting its data. (medium confidence) Sources: https://source.wiredtiger.com/develop/arch-checkpoint.html ; https://source.wiredtiger.com/develop/arch-eviction.html

Dirty-page write cost includes more than journal appends: the developer explanation describes copy-on-write data-file placement and per-table metadata synchronization; Percona also identifies CPU demand from compression during eviction. Both storage bandwidth and CPU capacity belong in checkpoint-cost diagnosis. (medium confidence) Sources: https://groups.google.com/g/wiredtiger-users/c/zNVzB6ZrYt4/m/YHjzWb2ECQAJ ; https://www.percona.com/blog/tuning-mongodb-for-bulk-loads/

The 2020 IBM Research study of WiredTiger and RocksDB distinguishes database-generated write amplification from SSD-internal write amplification. It shows that short tests, drive state, dataset size, and device technology can distort cost and throughput comparisons; its standalone-engine results do not establish a MongoDB deployment cost multiplier. (low confidence)
